note: Every capture is 45 s of the reference window at 30 fps. rate_from_median_gap is the figure method.md fixed - steps or turns a second from the median gap between them - and rate_over_span is (count-1)/span for comparison. keys_per_s_nominal is how fast the driving loop sent keys: the three walk windows all used the same loop at a nominal ten a second; the pass windows differ, p1 at about seventeen against ten for p2 and p3.

keypace_reference.program: keypace.asm, built with the repo-pinned NASM 2.16.03
keypace_reference.note: Keys the guest received through INT 16h, with the BIOS tick at each. The rig can saturate Ultima VI; a held key reaches 86Box as one keystroke.
keypace_reference.rate_formula: (n-1)/(last-first) over the tick list the program prints; SPAN includes the priming tap that starts the timing and must not be used as the denominator.

burst_walk_bw3.verdict: void: the route ran out of floor
burst_walk_bw3.why: Each leg walked one direction for several seconds. A saturated walk crosses a room in seconds: w4 took the Avatar out of the throne room into the next room, w6 found a wall at once and gave no steps. An earlier reading blamed the step counter for merging fast steps; the counts do not support it (8 events against walk_rate.py's 6 on w4).
burst_walk_bw3.what_is_needed: the one-tile square route the earlier windows used, which never leaves a tile
burst_walk_bw3.speed_gate: the four windows keyed at 25/s held 100% for all 240 frames; the four at 48.8/s ran at 71-101% under other work on the shared host and would have failed it

saturated_square_walk_reference.machine: 86Box award286 at 12.5 MHz, one wait state
saturated_square_walk_reference.window: 10 s of keys inside a 14 s capture at 30 fps; the Avatar walked round a one-tile square (down, right, up, left) so the route never runs out of floor

gates.out_of_combat: w-fightcheck grab: no hostile in the map view, no wound message
gates.emulation_speed: 100% for every frame of all six windows (speed_check.py: one distinct crop, 419-420 frames each)

saturation.reading: Not usable. The over-keyed figure is steady (12.3 and 25 a second agree to 0.53%) but it sits below what the same machine on the same route gave at 10 a second, so excess queued keys suppress steps and the steady figure is a rate the game can be held down to, not one it can reach. This does not show that no usable plateau exists: the peak lies somewhere below 12.3 keys a second, and neither the range under 10 nor the gap between 10 and 12.3 was sampled.

saturated_square_walk_reference.verdict: the over-keyed rate is suppressed, so it is not walking speed; not measured

standard_errors.note: two independent three-window means combine in quadrature, which is level with the plus/minus 10% band on its own

saturated_square_walk_kit.why: The command file inserted KEYPACE.COM before the game, but the kit image boots to a menu, not a DOS prompt, so the typing went into the menu and everything after it desynchronised: the grabs show COMMAND.COM answering "Bad command or filename" to the mangled lines, including "ultima6\". All six windows are a static DOS prompt (no frame-to-frame change at all).
saturated_square_walk_kit.consequence: The run also left Kit B with its lease blocked and the core loaded: the command file was missing its final quit, so the runner sat in its idle wait, and the run's post-run tail was then run by hand too early. The agent's cleanup then failed with HTTP 500, most likely because of that early removal, though that is not shown. A warm reboot cleared it, at Deano's word: the lease status is in-memory only, so any restart of the agent clears a blocked lease, while a maintenance-reservation block would persist. A takeover is refused HTTP 409 on a blocked lease, so no stop could be sent. The kit was restored, verified against the baseline and released; no reimage, boot-config change, I2C or power cycle.

slow_windows_both_counters.note: method.md's correction to the seventh amendment: the two counters agree, which is what rules out saturation
